> **Extra session (beyond the course).** This lab is for interest and is **not part of the
> final exam**. Part A treats forecasting as supervised learning with a random forest
> (`ranger`). Part B looks at stock returns and fits ARCH/GARCH models (`fGarch`).

# Packages

```{r}
library(fpp3)
has_ranger <- requireNamespace("ranger", quietly = TRUE)
has_fgarch <- requireNamespace("fGarch", quietly = TRUE)
if (has_fgarch) library(fGarch)   # attach: its coef(), predict(), residuals() methods are S4
c(ranger = has_ranger, fGarch = has_fgarch)
```

# Part A: time series and machine learning

## Data: Australian cafe turnover

Monthly turnover of cafes, restaurants and takeaway food services, all states, 2004-2018.
We work on the log scale, as in earlier sessions.

```{r}
cafe <- aus_retail |>
  filter(Industry == "Cafes, restaurants and takeaway food services",
         year(Month) %in% 2004:2018) |>
  summarise(Turnover = sum(Turnover))
cafe |> autoplot(Turnover) + labs(title = "Australian cafe turnover", y = "$ million")
```

## From a series to a supervised-learning table

`embed(z, p + 1)` returns a matrix whose first column is $z_t$ and whose next $p$ columns
are $z_{t-1}, \dots, z_{t-p}$: one row per time point, lags as features.

```{r}
z <- log(cafe$Turnover)
E <- embed(z, 12 + 1)
colnames(E) <- c("y", paste0("lag", 1:12))
head(round(E[, 1:5], 3))
dim(E)
```

A linear regression on this table is an AR(12) estimated by least squares:

```{r}
coef(lm(y ~ ., data = as.data.frame(E)))[1:4]
```

A random forest replaces the linear combination with averages of regression trees.

## Recursive forecasting with a random forest

The function fits a forest on the lag table, then forecasts one step at a time and feeds
each forecast back in as the newest lag.

```{r}
rf_recursive <- function(z, h, p = 12, seed = 2026) {
  E <- embed(z, p + 1)
  colnames(E) <- c("y", paste0("lag", 1:p))
  set.seed(seed)
  m <- ranger::ranger(y ~ ., data = as.data.frame(E), num.trees = 500)
  hz <- z
  out <- numeric(h)
  for (i in seq_len(h)) {
    nd <- as.data.frame(t(rev(tail(hz, p))))   # newest value is lag1
    names(nd) <- paste0("lag", 1:p)
    out[i] <- predict(m, nd)$predictions
    hz <- c(hz, out[i])                         # feed the forecast back in
  }
  out
}

# (a) forest on log levels
rf_levels <- function(y, h) rf_recursive(y, h)

# (b) forest on the seasonal difference of the log, then undo the difference:
#     y_t = y_{t-12} + w_t
rf_sdiff <- function(y, h) {
  wf <- rf_recursive(diff(y, lag = 12), h)
  hy <- y
  for (i in seq_len(h)) hy <- c(hy, hy[length(hy) - 11] + wf[i])
  tail(hy, h)
}
```

## One split: train to 2016, test 2017-2018

```{r}
train <- cafe |> filter(year(Month) <= 2016)
test <- cafe |> filter(year(Month) >= 2017)
h <- nrow(test)

fc_stat <- train |>
  model(snaive = SNAIVE(log(Turnover)),
        ets = ETS(log(Turnover)),
        arima = ARIMA(log(Turnover))) |>
  forecast(h = h)
acc <- accuracy(fc_stat, cafe) |> select(.model, RMSE)
acc
```

```{r, eval = has_ranger}
ly <- log(train$Turnover)
fc_ml <- tibble(Month = test$Month,
                rf_levels = exp(rf_levels(ly, h)),
                rf_sdiff = exp(rf_sdiff(ly, h)))
rmse <- function(f) sqrt(mean((test$Turnover - f)^2))
acc_all <- bind_rows(acc, tibble(.model = c("rf_levels", "rf_sdiff"),
                                 RMSE = c(rmse(fc_ml$rf_levels), rmse(fc_ml$rf_sdiff))))
acc_all |> arrange(RMSE)
```

## Trees cannot extrapolate

A tree predicts an average of training targets, so the forest on levels can never go above
the largest value it has seen.

```{r, eval = has_ranger}
c(train_max = max(train$Turnover),
  rf_levels_max = max(fc_ml$rf_levels),
  test_max = max(test$Turnover))

fc_ml |>
  pivot_longer(-Month, names_to = "model", values_to = "Turnover") |>
  ggplot(aes(Month, Turnover, colour = model)) +
  geom_line(data = cafe |> filter(year(Month) >= 2012) |> as_tibble(),
            aes(Month, Turnover), colour = "black", inherit.aes = FALSE) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = max(train$Turnover), linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(title = "Random forest forecasts, 2017-2018",
       subtitle = "Dashed line: largest value in the training data", y = "$ million")
```

Modelling the seasonal difference turns an extrapolation problem (a growing level) into
an interpolation problem (changes that stay in a familiar range). This is the same idea as
$d$ and $D$ in ARIMA.

## Rolling origins: is the forest really better?

One hold-out is one draw. Repeat the comparison for five forecast origins
(train up to 2012, ..., 2016; test the next 2 years each time).

```{r, eval = has_ranger}
run_origin <- function(end_year) {
  tr <- cafe |> filter(year(Month) <= end_year)
  te <- cafe |> filter(year(Month) %in% (end_year + 1):(end_year + 2))
  h <- nrow(te)
  st <- tr |>
    model(snaive = SNAIVE(log(Turnover)), ets = ETS(log(Turnover)),
          arima = ARIMA(log(Turnover))) |>
    forecast(h = h) |>
    accuracy(cafe) |>
    select(.model, RMSE)
  ly <- log(tr$Turnover)
  r <- function(f) sqrt(mean((te$Turnover - f)^2))
  bind_rows(st, tibble(.model = c("rf_levels", "rf_sdiff"),
                       RMSE = c(r(exp(rf_levels(ly, h))), r(exp(rf_sdiff(ly, h)))))) |>
    mutate(origin = end_year)
}
rolling <- bind_rows(lapply(2012:2016, run_origin))

rolling |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = origin, values_from = RMSE) |>
  mutate(mean = rowMeans(across(-.model))) |>
  arrange(mean) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), round))
```

```{r, eval = has_ranger}
rolling |>
  group_by(origin) |>
  slice_min(RMSE, n = 1) |>
  select(origin, winner = .model, RMSE)
```

**Read the table.** Which model wins the 2016 origin (the single split above)? Which model
has the lowest *mean* RMSE? How many origins does `rf_sdiff` win?

# Part B: time series in finance

## Prices and log returns

`gafa_stock` has daily prices for Apple, Amazon, Facebook and Google, 2014-2018. Trading
days are irregular (weekends, holidays), so we re-index by trading day, as in FPP3.
Returns are in percent: $r_t = 100\,(\log P_t - \log P_{t-1})$.

```{r}
aapl <- gafa_stock |>
  filter(Symbol == "AAPL") |>
  mutate(trading_day = row_number()) |>
  update_tsibble(index = trading_day, regular = TRUE) |>
  mutate(r = 100 * difference(log(Adj_Close))) |>
  filter(!is.na(r))

aapl |> autoplot(Adj_Close) + labs(title = "Apple adjusted close", y = "USD")
aapl |> autoplot(r) + labs(title = "Apple daily log returns", y = "%")
```

## Stylised facts

```{r}
aapl |> as_tibble() |>
  summarise(n = n(), mean = mean(r), sd = sd(r),
            kurtosis = mean((r - mean(r))^4) / sd(r)^4)
```

Kurtosis well above 3 means heavy tails: large moves are more common than a normal
distribution predicts.

```{r}
aapl |> ACF(r, lag_max = 30) |> autoplot() + labs(title = "ACF of returns")
aapl |> ACF(r^2, lag_max = 30) |> autoplot() + labs(title = "ACF of squared returns")
```

```{r}
aapl |> features(r, ljung_box, lag = 10)
aapl |> mutate(r2 = r^2) |> features(r2, ljung_box, lag = 10)
```

Returns themselves show little autocorrelation, but squared returns do: **volatility
clustering**. Engle's ARCH-LM test checks the same thing. `feasts::stat_arch_lm()` returns
the $R^2$ of a regression of $r_t^2$ on its lags; the test statistic is $n R^2$.

```{r}
arch <- aapl |> features(r, stat_arch_lm, lags = 10)
n <- nrow(aapl)
c(LM = n * arch$stat_arch_lm,
  p_value = pchisq(n * arch$stat_arch_lm, df = 10, lower.tail = FALSE))
```

## GARCH(1,1) by hand

$$
\sigma_t^2 = \omega + \alpha\,\varepsilon_{t-1}^2 + \beta\,\sigma_{t-1}^2
$$

The forecast recursion reverts to the long-run variance
$\bar\sigma^2 = \omega/(1-\alpha-\beta)$ at rate $\alpha+\beta$:

```{r}
omega <- 0.1; alpha <- 0.1; beta <- 0.8
sig2_bar <- omega / (1 - alpha - beta)
sig2_T1 <- omega + alpha * 3^2 + beta * 1.5        # shock 3, variance 1.5 today
hh <- 1:20
sig2_h <- sig2_bar + (alpha + beta)^(hh - 1) * (sig2_T1 - sig2_bar)
round(sig2_h[c(1, 2, 10, 20)], 3)
log(0.5) / log(alpha + beta)                          # half-life
```

## Fitting GARCH(1,1) to Apple returns

`garchFit()` fits a constant mean plus GARCH(1,1) errors by maximum likelihood.

```{r, eval = has_fgarch}
r <- aapl$r
g_norm <- garchFit(~ garch(1, 1), data = r, cond.dist = "norm", trace = FALSE)
cf <- coef(g_norm)
round(cf, 3)
pers <- unname(cf["alpha1"] + cf["beta1"])
c(persistence = pers,
  half_life_days = log(0.5) / log(pers),
  longrun_daily_sd = sqrt(unname(cf["omega"]) / (1 - pers)),
  annualised_sd = sqrt(252) * sqrt(unname(cf["omega"]) / (1 - pers)))
```

## Conditional volatility

```{r, eval = has_fgarch}
aapl_g <- aapl |> mutate(sigma = volatility(g_norm))
aapl_g |>
  ggplot(aes(trading_day)) +
  geom_line(aes(y = r), colour = "grey50") +
  geom_line(aes(y = cf["mu"] + 2 * sigma), colour = "red") +
  geom_line(aes(y = cf["mu"] - 2 * sigma), colour = "red") +
  labs(title = "Apple returns with GARCH(1,1) ±2 conditional sd",
       x = "Trading day", y = "%")
```

## Diagnostics

If the model captures the volatility dynamics, the squared **standardised** residuals
$\hat z_t^2 = (\hat\varepsilon_t / \hat\sigma_t)^2$ should show no autocorrelation.

```{r, eval = has_fgarch}
z <- residuals(g_norm, standardize = TRUE)
Box.test(z^2, lag = 10, type = "Ljung-Box")
c(kurtosis_z = mean((z - mean(z))^4) / sd(z)^4)
```

The clustering is gone, but $\hat z_t$ still has heavy tails, which motivates Student-$t$ errors.

## Volatility forecast

```{r, eval = has_fgarch}
vf <- predict(g_norm, n.ahead = 60)
tibble(h = 1:60, sd = vf$standardDeviation) |>
  ggplot(aes(h, sd)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = sqrt(cf["omega"] / (1 - pers)), linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(title = "GARCH(1,1) volatility forecast",
       subtitle = "Dashed line: long-run daily sd",
       x = "Days ahead", y = "Daily sd (%)")
```

## Student-t errors

```{r, eval = has_fgarch}
g_t <- garchFit(~ garch(1, 1), data = r, cond.dist = "std", trace = FALSE)
round(coef(g_t), 3)
rbind(normal = g_norm@fit$ics, student_t = g_t@fit$ics)[, c("AIC", "BIC")]
```

`fGarch` reports AIC per observation, so compare the two rows directly: lower is better.
`shape` is the degrees of freedom of the $t$ distribution.

# Your turn

1. **Lags.** Refit `rf_sdiff` with `p = 24` lags instead of 12. Does the mean rolling-origin
   RMSE improve?
2. **Another learner.** Replace the forest with a linear model on the same lag table
   (`lm(y ~ ., ...)`). How does this "AR(12) on seasonal differences" compare with
   `rf_sdiff` and with `ARIMA()`?
3. **Leakage.** Suppose you add a feature "mean of $y$ over the 12 months *centred* on $t$".
   Why would this give an excellent test RMSE and useless real forecasts?
4. **Another stock.** Repeat Part B for Amazon (`"AMZN"`). Compare $\alpha$, $\beta$,
   persistence and half-life with Apple.
5. **ARCH vs GARCH.** Fit `~ garch(1, 0)` (an ARCH(1)) to Apple returns. Compare its AIC
   with GARCH(1,1). Does the Ljung-Box test on $\hat z_t^2$ still pass?
6. **Interpretation.** If $\alpha + \beta = 0.99$, what is the half-life of a volatility
   shock? What does that say about how long a turbulent market stays turbulent?
